title: Allahabad Vendor's One-Rupee Mini Samosas Win Hearts After 22 Years
excerpt: A Prayagraj street vendor's bite-sized samosas, priced at just Re 1 each for a reported 22 years and served with green chutney, have become social media's latest street-food sensation.
body:
• A street vendor in Allahabad (Prayagraj) has gone viral for selling bite-sized samosas at just Re 1 each — a price he has reportedly held for nearly 22 years.
  • The tiny, crispy samosas are served with green chutney, and a recent Instagram reel by food creators Sahil & Priyanka brought the stall wider attention.
  • The story is a throwback in an age of inflation: a snack with a history stretching from medieval Central Asia to Mughal courts, now sold for a single rupee.
  • The 22-year claim comes from the viral post itself and has not been independently documented, so it is best read as the vendor's own account.

In a city famous for its sangam, it is a tiny triangle of pastry that is making waves. A street vendor in Allahabad — now Prayagraj — has caught the attention of food lovers across social media for selling miniature samosas at just Re 1 apiece, a price he has reportedly maintained for nearly 22 years, according to NDTV Food.

The bite-sized samosas, served with green chutney, were featured in an Instagram reel by food content creators Sahil & Priyanka, who showed the vendor preparing and serving the small, crispy snacks. Their size and their almost unbelievable price have made them an instant favourite among street-food fans online.

From royal courts to a one-rupee street snack

There is an irony in the story that food historians would appreciate: the samosa was not originally Indian at all. Its early relatives trace back to West and Central Asia, where medieval Arabic cookbooks from around the 10th to 13th centuries describe pastries called sanbusak and sanbusaj. The snack travelled trade routes into the subcontinent, and by the Delhi Sultanate period it was part of court cuisine — the 14th-century traveller Ibn Battuta wrote of sambusak served at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq, filled then with minced meat, nuts, onions and spices rather than potato.

The potato filling came much later, after the Columbian exchange brought the tuber to India and local cooks folded it in with peas and Indian spices. What emerged is the version found everywhere today, from railway platforms to wedding buffets — and, apparently, in miniature form on a Prayagraj street for the price of a single rupee.

Why a one-rupee samosa resonates

At a time when even a simple tea-and-snack break can add up, a Re 1 samosa feels like a dispatch from another era. Part of the appeal is pure economics: it is a working snack for working people, priced so that nobody has to think twice. Part of it is authenticity — there is no branding exercise here, no limited-edition menu, just a vendor, a kadhai and a crowd that has kept coming back for two decades.

It also fits the way India now discovers food. A short reel, a charismatic vendor and an eye-catching detail — in this case, the price — can turn a neighbourhood stall into a national talking point overnight. Whether the stall becomes a food-tourism stop or simply enjoys its moment, the formula is the same one that has powered countless street-food discoveries: real food, real people, no filter.

A word of caution, though. The exact daily sales, ingredients and price history of the stall are not independently documented in the available coverage; the 22-year claim comes from the viral post itself. That does not make it untrue — it makes it the vendor's story, carried by the people filming and sharing it.

A diaspora connection

For the Indian diaspora, the samosa is arguably the single most recognisable snack — the thing that shows up at every potluck, every Diwali party, every office celebration. A story like this lands because it is the samosa stripped to its essence: hot, crisp, cheap and eaten standing up. It is a reminder of the street food that no restaurant version, however polished, quite manages to replace.

What's next

For travellers passing through Prayagraj, the stall — reported to be in the Mumfordganj area — is now on the food-lover's map. For everyone else, NDTV Food's version of the story includes a full home recipe for mini samosas: a stiff maida dough with ajwain, a spiced potato-and-pea filling, and a slow fry on low heat until golden. The price may not be replicable at home, but the crunch is.

nri_angle: The samosa is the diaspora's most recognisable snack, and this story resonates as the samosa stripped to its essence — hot, crisp and cheap — a taste of street food no restaurant version quite replaces.
